title: Maitreyi's question and the breath of the Vedas
hookLine: Maitreyi turns down a fortune to ask what doesn't die, and hears where the Vedas come from.
carry: the vedas are shruti: heard, breathed out by brahman
tomorrow: a young monk, a ritual master, two garlands. whose wilts first?

cards: The sage Yajnavalkya is about to leave home life behind. He has two wives, Maitreyi and Katyayani, and he offers to settle his property between them before he goes. Maitreyi stops him.
If this whole earth, full of wealth, were mine, she asks, would it make me immortal? No, he says. You'd live the way rich people live.
That's all. Then what would I do with something that won't make me immortal? Tell me what you know.
So he does. And in the middle of that teaching, he says where the Vedas come from.

teach.b: Here's the line, in paraphrase: as smoke billows from a fire of damp wood, so the Rig Veda and the other Vedas are the breathing out of this great being.
That's the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, and it sits under one of Hinduism's central beliefs.

The Vedas are shruti, which means what was heard. Much of the tradition holds that no human sat down and composed them. The ancient rishis heard them, and passed them on mouth to ear for many centuries.
That's why a priest at a wedding or a thread ceremony chants Vedic verses exactly, sound by sound: the words are treated as received, not invented.
The third sutra builds on this. Shastra yonitvat. Shastra is scripture; yoni is source.
Shankara reads it two ways and keeps both. Brahman is the source of scripture, breathing it out without effort. And scripture is the source of knowing Brahman, which reasoning alone can't reach.

Out, and back again. So in Shankara's school, the path of jnana starts with listening: hearing the Upanishads from a teacher, reflecting on them, then dwelling on them until they're one's own. Maitreyi did exactly that.
She set down a fortune and asked to hear. Other schools weigh scripture and reasoning differently, and they've argued it out with care.

how: Vedic verses are still learned by ear, teacher to student, and chanted with exact sounds at rites like weddings and the thread ceremony; in Advaita Vedanta, students come to knowledge of Brahman through hearing the Upanishads from a teacher (shravana), reflecting on them (manana) and dwelling on them deeply (nididhyasana).

o: knowledge worked out by reasoning, with no scripture
knowledge kept secret by priests from everyone else
knowledge that begins by hearing the scriptures

games.q: Maitreyi's question and the third sutra. tap the pairs.
p: asked for what makes one immortal, not wealth
the breathing out of a great being

s: tradition says one poet sat down and wrote the Vedas
they're shruti, 'heard': much of the tradition holds no human composed them; the rishis heard them and passed them on.
Maitreyi turned down a share of wealth to ask about what doesn't die
would a whole earth of wealth make me immortal? no. then tell me what you know.
for Shankara, clever reasoning alone is enough to reach Brahman
Shankara reads the third sutra this way: Brahman isn't reached by inference alone; the Upanishads are how it's known.

games.q: two students argue over shastra yonitvat. one says Brahman is the source of scripture; the other says scripture is the source of knowing Brahman. you're Shankara. who's right?
o: both: the sutra can be read both ways.
only the first; the second is a misreading.
only the second; Brahman can't be a source.
games.why: Shankara gives both readings. Brahman breathes out the scripture, and the scripture leads back to knowing Brahman.

practice: If your family has a prayer or a mantra, say it once, slowly, aloud or under your breath, and listen to each sound as something handed down to you, not made up by you.
If you don't pray, sit tall with your hands open and let three out-breaths leave without pushing, the way the Upanishad pictures the Vedas, breathed out.

wordCard.voice: Jnana: knowledge that frees. In the third sutra, it starts with listening: scripture flows out of Brahman, and leads back to knowing it.

orig.note: Sanskrit shruti, what was heard; the name for the Vedas as revealed, not composed.

carryVoice: Pocket this, from Maitreyi's teacher: the Vedas are shruti, heard, breathed out by Brahman. Back here tomorrow.

sources.ref: Brahma Sutra 1.1.3 (shastra-yonitvat: because of being the source of scripture / because scripture is the source)
Shankara, Brahma Sutra Bhashya 1.1.3 (two readings: Brahman as the omniscient source of the scriptures, which are like a lamp; scripture as the means of knowing Brahman)
sources.work: Shankara, commentary on the Brahma Sutras (paraphrased)

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.1–3 (Yajnavalkya, about to leave, offers to settle his property between Maitreyi and Katyayani; Maitreyi asks whether an earth full of wealth would make her immortal, and asks to be taught) and 2.4.10 (as smoke from a fire of damp fuel, the Rig Veda and the rest are the breathing out of this great being)
